o: Count how often each value occurs; a value qualifies if no other value shares its frequency. Scan left to right and return the first qualifying element. In Example 1, frequencies are 20:1, 10:1, 30:2 — frequency 2 is unique, so 30 wins despite appearing later. In Example 2, all three frequencies are distinct, so the first element 20 wins. In Example 3, both values appear twice, so nothing qualifies and we return -1. With n up to 1e5, hash-map counting gives O(n).
k: Two counting passes: value -> frequency, then frequency -> number of values with that frequency.
A value qualifies iff its frequency is claimed by exactly one value.

a.i: Build the frequency map, invert it into a map from frequency to how many values have it, then scan the original array and return the first element whose frequency count is 1.
s: Count occurrences of each value with a hash map.
Count, for each frequency f, how many values have frequency f.
Scan nums in order; return the first x with count-of-frequency(count[x]) == 1.
a.t: O(n) — two counting passes plus one scan.

a.i: Since 1 <= nums[i] <= 1e5, plain arrays replace hash maps, cutting constant factors and avoiding hashing overhead.
s: Allocate count array of size 100001 and tally.
Allocate freqCount array; for each value present, increment freqCount[count[v]].
Scan nums; return first x with freqCount[count[x]] == 1, else -1.
a.t: O(n + V) where V = 100001 — counting plus a scan over the value range.
a.sp: O(n + V) for the two counting arrays.

w: Either approach is fine; mention the array variant when values are bounded. Pitfall: confusing 'first element with a frequency of 1' with 'first element whose frequency is unique' — read carefully. Edge cases: all elements identical (frequency shared by one value — is a lone frequency 'unique'? Here yes, since no other integer shares it), and empty qualifying sets returning -1. Follow-up: return the k-th such element, or handle streaming updates.
